4.text: If some serious misfortune happens, the people of the nearest camp will

5.text: always give help; the more so, since they are in most cases relatives, or at

6.text: least good friends. As an instance may be given the following story, where

7.text: the sudden death of a Chukchee while hunting wild reindeer is described.

8.text: “When he left the camp and followed the reindeer-buck, they both ran to the ice on a large

9.text: lake. He slipped on the ice and fell down. Here he broke his neck and remained on the ice.

10.text: Two nights he was absent from his camp. After the second night, his wife went to the neighbors

11.text: and brought them the news: ‘My husband is absent!’ — ‘Oh, where is he?’ — ‘He was following the

12.text: wounded reindeer.’ — ‘Oh, oh! let us go and look for him.... Well, do you know what direction

13.text: we are to take?’ They went together, the woman and one of the neighbors. The woman sought

14.text: on the land. He took the road across the ice. Then he found him, and gave a signal to the

15.text: woman, who also came. The dead man was lying on the ice.”¹

16.text: Neighboring camps often, in changing the pasture-grounds, follow the

17.text: same route, in order to keep all the time in the same neighborhood as before.

18.text: They gather their skins and peltries and give them to one man, who goes

19.text: to some distant place for trading-purposes. They also assemble for ceremonials

26.text: the strongest”). The front house belongs to the family which has lived at

27.text: the place longest without interruption. I spoke before of the fluctuation of

28.text: the population in the maritime villages, according as luck in hunting changed.

29.text: Now, a family like this remains in its place even under the most trying con-

30.text: ditions. Their intimate knowledge of the place makes it possible for them

31.text: to provide for their subsistence in one way or another. The position of this

32.text: house will be in front of the others; i. e., on the right side of the line of

33.text: houses, which are all turned with the entrance towards the sea. I have

34.text: already mentioned that in several villages the owner of the front house pretends

35.text: to have the priority of connection with the local gods, and even receives

36.text: occasionally a kind of tribute from the other families.² Many villages, however,

37.text: some of them among the largest, have no front house at all. In these, all

38.text: the inhabitants are on a quite equal footing, and the houses are scattered
